nodes.title: Katz cyclic-vector candidate
nodes.statement: For a rank-n differential module with ordered basis e₀,…,eₙ₋₁ over R, define c(e,x)=Σ₀≤j<n (x^j/j!) Σ₀≤k≤j (−1)^k binom(j,k) D^k(e_(j−k)). The rank-zero candidate is zero. This is an explicit candidate, not an assertion that every x works.
hypotheses: R is a commutative differential ring; D is additive and satisfies D(rv)=∂(r)v+rD(v).
(n−1)! is invertible when n>0; x=t−a with ∂t=1 and ∂a=0 for the cyclic-vector theorem.
proofSteps: Form the finite sums on the existing module carrier; keep the connection constant-linear.
Use the binomial cancellation in its first n differential jets; do not define cyclicity again, since the main packet already owns it.

nodes.title: Katz determinant criterion
nodes.statement: With ∂t=1, the formal candidate in R[X] equipped with ∂X=1 has Wronskian P(X)=det(c,Dc,…,D^(n−1)c) in the e-basis, with P(0)=1 and degree at most n(n−1). If P(t−a) is a unit, c(e,t−a) is cyclic.
hypotheses: n>0; (n−1)! invertible; R commutative; e a basis; the connection extends to R[X] by Leibniz.
proofSteps: Expand the j-th jet. Binomial cancellation leaves eⱼ at X=0, giving the identity coordinate matrix.
Each jet column has X-degree at most n−1, so the determinant has degree at most n(n−1).
Specialisation at X=t−a commutes with D exactly when a is constant. Invertibility of the determinant is the basis criterion.

sources.match: The constant term and determinant degree give both the local criterion and the finite-family algorithm.

acceptance: The Wronskian at X=0 is 1, not merely nonzero.
Track the differential structure on the polynomial variable; ordinary coefficientwise differentiation would fail.

nodes.title: Katz cyclic-vector algorithm
nodes.statement: If R is local and t−a lies in its maximal ideal, c(e,t−a) is cyclic. More generally, if constants contain a field k with at least N=n(n−1)+1 elements, any N distinct constants aᵢ yield candidates whose cyclic loci cover Spec R. Over a differential field of characteristic zero with ∂t=1, at least one of these candidates is cyclic.
hypotheses: n>0; finite free rank n; the factorial assumption of katz-candidate.
For the global conclusion k⊂ker ∂ is a field and N pairwise distinct aᵢ belong to k.
proofSteps: Locally the determinant reduces to 1 modulo the maximal ideal.
Globally evaluate P at t−aᵢ. The Vandermonde determinant is a product of nonzero constant differences, hence a unit.
Since P has degree ≤N−1 and constant term 1, its coefficients, and therefore the evaluation values, generate the unit ideal. Each prime admits an invertible evaluation after localisation.

sources.match: The field proof is obtained from a finite covering by explicit candidates, not by an unspecified generic vector.

acceptance: Use exactly N candidates, including N=1 in rank one.
The conclusion over a ring is local cyclicity, not necessarily one globally cyclic candidate.

nodes.title: Rescaling a nonzero derivation
nodes.statement: Over a characteristic-zero differential field with ∂≠0, choose t with s=∂t≠0. Put δ=s⁻¹∂ and D′=s⁻¹D. For every v, the spans of the first n iterates of D and D′ agree; cyclicity is unchanged. Hence the Katz algorithm applies with δt=1.
hypotheses: K a characteristic-zero field; D constant-linear with Leibniz rule; n is the finite rank.
proofSteps: Use the Leibniz rule to check D′ is a connection for δ.
Induction gives (D′)^i(v)=s^(−i)D^i(v) plus lower iterates. The transition matrix is triangular with nonzero diagonal.
Apply the finite-candidate theorem. With ∂=0 and D=0 on K² no vector is cyclic; do not drop ∂≠0.

sources.locator: pp. 65–67, ∂t=1 setup; rescaling argument supplied here
sources.match: The argument explicitly connects the normalised algorithm to the main cyclic-vector statement.

acceptance: The field hypothesis is needed to invert s.

nodes.title: Extrinsic subsidiary-radius variation
nodes.statement: For the ∂₀-connection, order subsidiary radii R₁≤…≤R_d; set fᵢ(r)=−log Rᵢ(M,e^(−r)) and Fᵢ=Σⱼ≤i fⱼ. All fᵢ and Fᵢ are continuous and piecewise affine; Fᵢ is convex, and its affine slopes are integral whenever i=d or fᵢ>fᵢ₊₁. In general slopes of fᵢ lie in the union of (1/e)ℤ for 1≤e≤d. On a disc, slopes of Fᵢ are nonpositive where fᵢ>r, and fᵢ=r for sufficiently large r.
hypotheses: K is a complete nonarchimedean characteristic-zero field, with positive residue characteristic p, commuting rational-type coefficient derivations ∂₁,…,∂ₘ and parameters uⱼ.
∂ⱼuⱼ=1, ∂ⱼuₖ=0 for j≠k, ‖∂ⱼ‖=|uⱼ|⁻¹ and the rational-type factorial bounds hold; ∂₀=d/dt.
M is a nonzero finite locally free coherent module with the indicated continuous integrable connection on A¹_K(I), rank d. η=e^(−r) lies in I.
proofSteps: Reduce at small radii to a cyclic twisted polynomial and its Newton polygon; use the imported spectral and transfer statements.
For nonvisible radii use Frobenius pushforward/antecedents and recover individual slopes by subtracting partial sums.
The full ∂₀ argument in KX is a reference to book Theorem 11.3.2; gap G1 records the unverified analytic input rather than declaring this proof closed.

sources.match: This is the extrinsic profile, with eventual fᵢ=r on a disc.

acceptance: A trivial ∂₀-line has R=η and f=r.
Order f₁≥…≥f_d; do not sum the smallest negative logarithms.

nodes.title: Coefficient-derivation radius variation
nodes.statement: For a fixed coefficient derivation ∂ⱼ, define fᵢ and Fᵢ from extrinsic ∂ⱼ subsidiary radii as above. They are continuous, Fᵢ is convex, and they are piecewise affine wherever fᵢ>−log|uⱼ|. On the region fᵢ>(log p)/(p^n(p−1))−log|uⱼ|, slopes of Fᵢ at a total sum or strict gap lie in p^(−n)ℤ and individual slopes lie in the union of (1/(p^n e))ℤ, 1≤e≤d. On a disc Fᵢ has nonpositive slopes.
hypotheses: K is a complete nonarchimedean characteristic-zero field, with positive residue characteristic p, commuting rational-type coefficient derivations ∂₁,…,∂ₘ and parameters uⱼ.
∂ⱼuⱼ=1, ∂ⱼuₖ=0 for j≠k, ‖∂ⱼ‖=|uⱼ|⁻¹ and the rational-type factorial bounds hold; ∂₀=d/dt.
M is a nonzero finite locally free coherent module with the indicated continuous integrable connection on A¹_K(I), rank d. η=e^(−r) lies in I.
j∈{1,…,m}; n≥0 in the visibility-threshold assertion.
proofSteps: Use an almost-isometric basis and a cyclic vector for ∂ⱼ. The visible spectral radii come from the coefficient Newton polygon (KX Lemmas 2.2.2–2.2.3).
Away from visibility apply the ∂ⱼ-Frobenius pushforward, separate its subsidiary spectrum and induct on the threshold n; the scaling introduces p^(−n).
Continuity follows from the spectral norms; convexity follows from the Newton polygon and induction. The isometric-basis and contraction suppliers cited only to the unread book remain G1.

sources.locator: Theorem 2.2.6 and proof, pp. 20–22; Lemmas 2.2.2–2.2.3, pp. 19–20
sources.match: The coefficient theorem has a visibility restriction; it alone does not supply strong intrinsic integrality.

acceptance: Do not claim piecewise affinity at fᵢ=−log|uⱼ| from this theorem alone.

nodes.title: Intersection descent of annular projectors
nodes.statement: For domains R=S∩T inside U and a finite locally free R-module M, M=(M⊗S)∩(M⊗T) inside M⊗U. An idempotent endomorphism on M⊗S extending an idempotent on M⊗T descends uniquely to M. Thus compatible spectral projectors on overlapping annular charts glue.
hypotheses: All maps are injective; R=S∩T is an actual ring-intersection statement in the common overring U.
M is finite locally free, not just torsion-free.
proofSteps: For v in the intersection define the ideal of denominators making v lie in M; localisation on a trivialising cover shows this ideal is the unit ideal.
Apply the intersection result to End_R(M), which is finite locally free.
Descend the operator and its equation P²=P using injectivity; uniqueness supplies agreement on overlaps.

sources.match: The local-free intersection argument is the algebraic engine for gluing decompositions.

acceptance: The image and kernel are locally free direct summands.
Correct the self-reference in Lemma 2.3.2 to Lemma 2.3.1; do not assume all open-annular modules globally free.

nodes.title: Affine-gap extrinsic annular splitting
nodes.statement: On an open annulus A¹_K(α,β) with α>0, if Fᵢ for one derivation is affine on (−logβ,−logα) and fᵢ>fᵢ₊₁ throughout, 1≤i<d, there is a unique differential direct-sum decomposition whose first summand has exactly the first i subsidiary radii at every η.
hypotheses: K is a complete nonarchimedean characteristic-zero field, with positive residue characteristic p, commuting rational-type coefficient derivations ∂₁,…,∂ₘ and parameters uⱼ.
∂ⱼuⱼ=1, ∂ⱼuₖ=0 for j≠k, ‖∂ⱼ‖=|uⱼ|⁻¹ and the rational-type factorial bounds hold; ∂₀=d/dt.
M is a nonzero finite locally free coherent module with the indicated continuous integrable connection on A¹_K(I), rank d. η=e^(−r) lies in I.
Fix ∂₀ or one ∂ⱼ; no assertion of global freeness for either summand.
proofSteps: On closed subannuli use affine log norms at a Newton-polygon vertex to obtain unit coefficients and two coprime characteristic factors (KX Lemmas 2.3.3–2.3.4).

In the visible coefficient case the separation of factors gives a spectral projector by an iterative contraction; the quantitative contraction is the unread book input G1. The ∂₀ branch is book Theorem 12.4.2.

acceptance: Removing affineness is not licensed by a pointwise spectral gap.

nodes.title: Intrinsic subsidiary-radius variation
nodes.statement: For the full commuting connection, order intrinsic subsidiary radii IR₁≤…≤IR_d≤1 and put fᵢ=−log IRᵢ and Fᵢ=Σⱼ≤i fⱼ. All profiles are continuous and piecewise affine; Fᵢ is convex and has integral slopes at i=d or a strict gap fᵢ>fᵢ₊₁. Individual slopes lie in the union of (1/e)ℤ, 1≤e≤d. On a disc Fᵢ has nonpositive slopes and is constant for sufficiently large r.
hypotheses: K is a complete nonarchimedean characteristic-zero field, with positive residue characteristic p, commuting rational-type coefficient derivations ∂₁,…,∂ₘ and parameters uⱼ.
∂ⱼuⱼ=1, ∂ⱼuₖ=0 for j≠k, ‖∂ⱼ‖=|uⱼ|⁻¹ and the rational-type factorial bounds hold; ∂₀=d/dt.
M is a nonzero finite locally free coherent module with the indicated continuous integrable connection on A¹_K(I), rank d. η=e^(−r) lies in I.
proofSteps: Use the half-open local decompositions of KX Theorems 2.3.8–2.3.10 to partition constituents according to their dominant derivation near a radius; their precise analytic inputs are included in G1.
Rotate a coefficient-dominant block into a t-block and apply the extrinsic strong-integrality theorem.
If θᵢ is the number of t-dominant constituents among the first i, compare one-sided slopes: (Fᵢ,rot)′₊−θᵢ≤Fᵢ′₊ and (Fᵢ,rot)′₋−θᵢ≥Fᵢ′₋. This yields convexity and the integral partial slopes.
At the maximum radius, convexity and discrete possible slopes force local finite piecewise affinity. Transfer on a disc gives eventual constancy.

acceptance: A horizontal line has f=0, in contrast with the extrinsic f=r.

nodes.statement: On A¹_K(α,β), α>0, if the intrinsic Fᵢ is affine and fᵢ>fᵢ₊₁ throughout, there is a unique decomposition of M into integrable differential summands with the first i and remaining subsidiary intrinsic radii respectively.

nodes.title: Boundary break and Swan-integrality proof support
nodes.statement: For a module solvable at the outer boundary, the full intrinsic partial profiles are eventually affine with nonnegative rational slopes. The imported break decomposition is obtained by repeatedly splitting at strict gaps, and the total break multiplicity sum is integral.

nodes.title: Puiseux Newton-polygon root criterion
nodes.statement: For a nonzero finite polynomial P(z)=Σc_e z^e with distinct nonnegative rational exponents, a finite number l is the valuation of a nonzero root in an algebraically closed valued field if and only if the lower convex hull of (−e,v(c_e)) has a segment of slope l. A monomial has no nonzero root.
hypotheses: Zero coefficients are omitted; rational exponents have one common denominator; roots are evaluated after adjoining that denominator-th root.
proofSteps: Clear denominators in the exponents by z=w^N.
Apply the ordinary Newton-polygon root criterion and convert the slope back, accounting for the minus sign in the exponent coordinate.
Exclude z=0, whose valuation is infinite.

sources.locator: Lemma 4.11, published pp. 148–149; arXiv v4 pp. 51–52
sources.match: The finite fractional-polynomial criterion supplies the initial root and lifting steps in the key calculation.

acceptance: For z−a the segment slope is v(a).

nodes.title: Kedlaya monodromy key calculation
nodes.statement: In the algebraically closed extended analytic ring with invertible q-Frobenius σ fixing a uniformiser π, let n≥1 and x=Σᵢ₌₀ⁿuᵢπ^i, where the uᵢ are strong semiunits of negative residue valuation or zero and x≠0. There exist a,b, not both zero, with σ(a)=πa and πσ^n(b)=b−ax.
hypotheses: The extended-ring topology, strong-semiunit partial valuations and Frobenius action are those of RD.0.
The residue valuation is nontrivial; complete algebraically closed residue field; π is fixed by σ.
Normalise the π-adic contribution to w_ρ so w_ρ(π)=1 in the nonvanishing calculation.
proofSteps: For m>0 set f(i,l,m)=(v₀(uᵢ)+m q^(−l))q^(−n(i+l)), and h(m)=minᵢ,ₗ f(i,l,m). The minimum is locally finite, increasing, piecewise affine, and h(qm)=q^(−n)h(m). Choose a corner τ with h(τ)<0.
Define T by f(i,l,τ)<0, S by f(i,l,τ)<q^(−n)h(τ), and s(i,l)=floor(log_(q^n)(h(τ)/f(i,l,τ))). S is finite; s≥0, and only finitely many indices have bounded s.

On the uniformly bounded partial-valuation modules U_τ→U_h(τ), define the additive π-linear convergent operator r(z)=Σ_T π^s σ^(−ni−nl+ns)(uᵢ) σ^(−ni−(n+1)l+ns)(z). Its reduction is a finite Puiseux polynomial with distinct exponents. The corner supplies a nonzero root of valuation τ.

Lift every required reduction recursively modulo successive powers of π, keeping the same uniform valuation bound. Completeness and continuity then give a nonzero z with v₀(z)=τ and r(z)=0; dense image alone would not imply surjectivity.

Put a=Σₗ∈ℤπ^lσ^(−l)(z). Since z∈U_τ and v₀(z)=τ, w_ρ(π^lσ^(−l)(z))=l+ρq^(−l)τ. Choose 1/(q−1)<ρτ<q/(q−1): the l=0 term uniquely minimises the valuation, so a≠0. The valuations tend to infinity at both ends and σ(a)=πa. Split ax=A+B using T; B has nonnegative partial valuation. The nonnegative-valuation difference input (monodromy Proposition 3.19(d), pp. 126–127) writes B=πσ^n(b₁)−b₁: explicitly b₁=−Σₖ≥0π^kσ^(nk)(B). Nonnegative residue partial valuations and the increasing π powers guarantee its convergence, and finite sums telescope.

For each index in T, the oriented finite geometric sum of length i+l−s gives b₂ with A=r(z)+πσ^n(b₂)−b₂. The integers i+l−s are uniformly bounded, so all summation k lie in one finite set of integers. Each unshifted summand has every partial valuation ≥h(τ), and σ^(nk) multiplies this bound by one of finitely many q^(nk). The π shifts have a uniform lower index bound; bounded-s index sets are finite. These facts give a uniform residue-valuation lower bound, π-adic convergence and overconvergence. Set b=−b₁−b₂; since a≠0 the pair is nonzero. G2 records only the ordinary Newton-polygon supplier still missing.

nodes.title: Artin–Hasse integrality
nodes.statement: For each prime p, E_p(X)=exp(Σⱼ≥0 X^(p^j)/p^j) and its inverse have p-integral coefficients and constant coefficient 1.
hypotheses: Formal power series over Q_p; integrality means membership in Z_p[[X]].
proofSteps: Use the Euler product E_p(X)=∏_{m≥1,p∤m}(1−X^m)^(−μ(m)/m); the formal logarithm agrees coefficientwise by the Möbius divisor sum.
The exponents −μ(m)/m are p-adic integers. The binomial coefficients of a p-adic integer are integral, by density of ordinary nonnegative integers and continuity of the binomial polynomial.
Every fixed coefficient involves finitely many factors. Negating the exponents proves integrality of the inverse. This elementary proof is provided here; Dwork states the integrality input.

nodes.title: Dwork splitting-function overconvergence
nodes.statement: Let π^(p−1)=−p in a complete extension of Q_p, v_p(p)=1, and θ(X)=exp(π(X−X^p)) as a formal series. Both θ and θ⁻¹ have coefficients of degree k with valuation at least αk, where α=(p−1)/p²>0. Hence θ is an analytic unit on |X|<p^α. The imported Dwork module on the Robba annulus admits F(w)=θ(t⁻¹)⁻¹w with an overconvergent inverse.
hypotheses: p prime, including p=2; the analytic evaluation is of the extended formal series, not necessarily of the scalar exponential.
The coefficient Frobenius fixes π and sends t to t^p for this example.
proofSteps: Factor θ=E_p(πX)∏ⱼ≥2 exp(−π^(p^j)X^(p^j)/p^j); the X^p term cancels because π^p/p=−π.
For degree k p^j in the j-th exponential, v_p≥k((p^j−1)/(p−1)−j)≥α k p^j for j≥2. The E_p factor and its inverse have degree-d valuation ≥d/(p−1).
Finite coefficient convolutions preserve the α-degree bound. The same argument with signs reversed handles θ⁻¹. Their formal product is 1, so they are inverse analytic functions on the open disc.
Substitute X=t⁻¹ to obtain an annulus |t|>p^(−α), including inner radii below 1. Differentiate the Frobenius factor and verify the chain rule for D(w)=−πt⁻²w.

nodes.title: Descending bounded generic slope filtration
nodes.statement: Every finite-dimensional Frobenius module M over E† has a unique filtration by saturated Frobenius submodules whose completed graded pieces are isoclinic of strictly decreasing arithmetic slopes. The filtration completes to the decreasing generic slope filtration over E. If F is algebraically closed, every graded piece is a direct sum of standard E† blocks of its one slope; M itself need not be their direct sum.
hypotheses: F is a perfect complete nontrivially valued characteristic-p field; q is a power of p; σ raises residue coefficients to q-th powers and fixes π.
E† is the bounded overconvergent Teichmüller coefficient field and E its π-adic completion, in the Fargues–Fontaine §11.2.5 convention; the coefficient-ring identification is requested from RD.0.
Frobenius modules have invertible linearisation; this does not imply Frobenius is bijective on an arbitrary integral lattice.
proofSteps: Take the highest completed slope submodule. Its determinant is a rank-one Frobenius line in an exterior power.

In rank one choose λ with the highest slope and a completed eigenbasis vᵢ. Approximate it by bounded overconvergent wᵢ so λwᵢ=ΣⱼBᵢⱼF(wⱼ), with B mod π=diag(1,0,…,0). For v₁=Σcᵢwᵢ use σ(cᵢ)=ΣⱼBⱼᵢcⱼ. Choose r with w_r(B)≥0; induction in the π-index gives rv_h(cᵢ)+h≥0. At h=0 the coordinates reduce to δᵢ₁, not all to zero. Thus the determinant line has overconvergent coordinates. Apply the imported saturated exterior-power descent and the RD.0 intersection statement to descend from the algebraic extension.

Pass to the quotient and induct on rank. Completed uniqueness and injectivity give uniqueness over E†. For graded standard forms use the fixed-slope completion comparison, not full faithfulness on mixed slopes.

nodes.statement: For the FF analytic coefficient ring R_F=colim_(ρ→0) B_(0,ρ], restriction and Frobenius gluing identify finite projective Frobenius modules with compatible Frobenius bundles on the punctured analytic radius domain. nodes.title: Equal-characteristic extension section theorem
nodes.statement: Over the Hartl–Pink punctured-disc ring, for every r≥1 and every σ-bundle extension 0→O(−1)→G→F_(1,r)→0 there is a nonzero Frobenius-fixed section of G.
hypotheses: F is complete algebraically closed characteristic p with nontrivial norm; σ is coefficientwise q-power, fixes the Laurent variable z.
HP F_(d,r) has σ^r=z^(−d), geometric degree d and arithmetic slope −d/r.
proofSteps: Write the extension matrix [[z,b],[0,A_(1,r)]]. A section of the quotient has coordinates v_t=Σᵢ∈ℤz^(−i)w^(q^(ir−t)) for 0<|w|<1; the first coordinate u must solve u=zσ(u)+bσ(v).
Its forced coefficients are u_i=Σⱼ≥0 f_(i−j)^(q^j). The negative-power tail always converges; the positive tail is controlled by a fractional q-polynomial condition (HP Lemmas 9.3–9.4).

Reduce to HP Proposition 9.5. Discard residue-norm ≤1 coefficients and shift so m=Σ_l m_l z^l has only positive exponents, with log|m_l|≤cl. For n=r+1 form F_i(w)=Σ_(0<j<ni)F_(i,j)w^(q^(−j)), where F_(i,j)=Σ_(j/n<k≤i)m_(nk−j)^(q^(−k)). Their logarithmic profiles φ_(i,j)=log|F_(i,j)| satisfy φ_(i+l,j+nl)=q^(−l)φ_(i,j); the actual coefficient differences satisfy log|F_(i′,j)−F_(i,j)|≤cn i q^(−i) for i′≥i≥2.
If every limiting φ_j≤0, any sufficiently small nonzero w works. Otherwise choose a corner ρ≥cn of max_j(φ_j−q^(−j)ρ), with positive maximum at two j. Newton polygons yield roots w_i of norm exp(−ρ).

Use the ball-image criterion for additive fractional q-polynomials to choose compatible roots with log|w_(i+1)−w_i|≤−c′q^((n−1)i/2). Their limit w retains nonzero norm; splitting j at ni/2 gives limsup log|F_i(w)|≤0 and the required positive-tail convergence.

nodes.title: Equal-characteristic Frobenius classification
nodes.statement: For algebraically closed perfectoid F and E=F_q((π)), every finite projective Frobenius module over R_F is a direct sum of standard blocks with coprime integer pair (c,r), r>0, satisfying φ^r=π^c. The multiset of pairs is unique, and its arithmetic slope is c/r. With c=−d these are the Hartl–Pink blocks F_(d,r). Together with the imported mixed-characteristic classification, this covers the two coefficient characteristics in FF Remark 11.3.4, subject to the explicit ring comparison G3.

proofSteps: Use HP Theorem 4.1 to find a line subbundle of maximal degree; saturation and the degree bound make its quotient a σ-bundle. Rank-one classification and slope-ordered splitting are the imported standard/HN inputs transported to this coefficient category (G3).

Induct simultaneously: every degree-zero bundle has a section; every bundle splits into standard blocks; every nonnegative-degree bundle has a section. The nonsplit degree-zero obstruction is equalchar-degree-zero-section-input.

For rank r and degree d, pull back under [r] and twist by −d to obtain degree zero. A section yields a map from [r]_*O(d). If full rank, use saturation/degree and gcd(d,r); otherwise split off a standard summand by the slope inequality and induct.
HP Corollary 11.8 gives uniqueness. Transport through the germ comparison, preserving the sign c=−d and arithmetic slope convention.
